summary: The decree of destruction, in the king's own words — a masterpiece of imperial spin: Artaxerxes presents himself as a clement ruler, Aman as 'second after the king... whom we honour as a father,' and the Jews as a scattered people 'using new laws' who disturb the peace of all nations. Then the counter-text: Mordecai's prayer, denying pride — 'I feared lest I should transfer the honour of my God to a man' — and begging mercy for a people going down to hell in one day.
whyItMatters: Here the Greek additions do their deepest work. The Hebrew Esther never explains why Mordecai refused to bow; this chapter gives the reason — conscience before God — and puts a full prayer in the mouth of a man the Hebrew text never shows praying. The persecution gets a theology.

keyVerses.text: Told me that there was a people scattered through the whole world, which used new laws, and acted against the customs of all nations, despised the commandments of kings, and violated by their opposition the concord of all nations.
keyVerses.why: The eternal grammar of antisemitism, dictated by a courtier and signed by a king — 'a people whose laws are different.' The decree is quoted at length so the reader can watch the lie being built.

keyVerses.text: Thou knowest that it was not out of pride and contempt, or any desire of glory, that I refused to worship the proud Aman... But I feared lest I should transfer the honour of my God to a man, and lest I should adore any one except my God.
keyVerses.why: The reason for the whole catastrophe, stated by Mordecai himself: worship belongs to God alone.

keyVerses.text: Hear my supplication, and be merciful to thy lot and inheritance, and turn our mourning into joy, that we may live and praise thy name, O Lord, and shut not the mouths of them that sing to thee.
keyVerses.why: The prayer's goal — not survival for its own sake, but a people alive to praise. 'Turn our mourning into joy' becomes the feast of Purim's charter.

questions.question: Why quote the entire decree?
questions.answer: Documentary power: you hear the genocide ordered in the polished language of statecraft — clemency, peace, concord. The Hebrew book gives Haman's decree in one verse; the Greek makes you sit through the whole performance of righteous-sounding hatred. Propaganda is easier to recognize once you have read a full specimen.

questions.question: Why did Mordecai refuse to bow to Haman?
questions.answer: The Hebrew book never says; readers have guessed pride, office, or custom. This addition answers in Mordecai's own prayer: refusing to bow was worship-logic — 'I feared lest I should transfer the honour of my God to a man.' He even adds that he would have kissed Haman's feet for Israel's sake (13:13): it was never personal.

questions.question: Does God appear in the Hebrew Esther at all?
questions.answer: No — not once, not even the word. That silence is famous and deliberate: God hidden behind coincidences. The Greek additions answer the silence: prayers here name him constantly. The two texts together ask the book's real question — is God absent from Esther, or invisible?

questions.question: What does 'going down to hell in one day' mean?
questions.answer: The decree orders every Jew — 'with their wives and children' — killed on a single day, the thirteenth of Adar. 'Hell' translates the Greek hades, the grave: an entire people in the grave in one day. The scale is the point; so is the unity of the threat and, later, of the rescue.

questions.question: Why does Mordecai call God 'king' and 'God of Abraham'?
questions.answer: The titles stack the covenant history against the empire's power: 'O Lord, Lord, almighty king, for all things are in thy power' (13:9), then 'O God of Abraham' (13:15) — the God who began with one old man and a promise. Against 127 provinces stands one covenant.
